RETALIATION FOR FILING A WAGE CLAIM — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — ALLEGED RETALIATION FOR A WAGE CLAIM OR RELATED ACTIVITY
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment with Acme, Inc. The wage claim, Labor Commissioner-related activity, or other conduct I believe may be connected to an adverse action against me is described here as: Reported suspected wage-and-hour violations to the payroll manager. The adverse action I believe may be connected to that activity is described here as: The employee was demoted and had their hours reduced within two weeks of filing a workers’ compensation claim., which I understand to have occurred on August 15, 2026.

This information sheet describes California Labor Code section 98.6 — a statute that separately prohibits an employer from discharging, discriminating, or retaliating against an employee or applicant because of certain wage-claim, Labor Commissioner-related, and other statutorily listed conduct — along with the related administrative complaint process under Labor Code section 98.7. It is not a Labor Commissioner complaint, is not a civil complaint or any other court filing, is not filed with the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, any court, or any other agency by completing it, and does not initiate any proceeding. Completing it does not establish that Jordan Lee engaged in any conduct protected under Labor Code section 98.6, that Acme, Inc. took any adverse action because of that conduct, or that any specific fact stated here is true. Only a court, or the Labor Commissioner acting under Labor Code section 98.7, can determine whether a violation of Labor Code section 98.6 occurred.

THE CORE PROHIBITION AND THE STATUTE'S OWN LIST OF PROTECTED CONDUCT
California law prohibits an employer from discharging an employee, or in any manner discriminating, retaliating, or taking any adverse action against an employee or applicant for employment, because that person engaged in conduct this statute and a related chapter of the Labor Code delineate as protected. The statute's own text lists several distinct categories of protected conduct rather than a single one: engaging in conduct described elsewhere in the same statutory chapter, including whistleblower-type conduct addressed in a separate Labor Code provision; filing a bona fide complaint or claim, or instituting or causing to be instituted any proceeding, relating to rights under the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction; making a written or oral complaint that the person is owed unpaid wages; initiating an action or notice, or testifying or being about to testify, in a proceeding under the Labor Code's Private Attorneys General Act provision; and the exercise, on behalf of the employee or others, of any rights the statute affords.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A person shall not discharge an employee or in any manner discriminate, retaliate, or take any adverse action against any employee or applicant for employment because the employee or applicant engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter, including the conduct described in subdivision (k) of Section 96, and Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 1101) of Part 3 of Division 2, or because the employee or applicant for employment has filed a bona fide complaint or claim or instituted or caused to be instituted any proceeding under or relating to their rights that are under the jurisdiction of the Labor Commissioner, made a written or oral complaint that they are owed unpaid wages, or because the employee has initiated any action or notice pursuant to Section 2699, or has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding pursuant to that section, or because of the exercise by the employee or applicant for employment on behalf of themselves or others of any rights afforded them."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.6.)

No claim is made about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, or that any specific complaint, activity, or exercise of rights actually falls within this statute's coverage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific adverse action was taken because of protected conduct, or that a violation of Labor Code § 98.6 occurred in this or any specific case.

THE REMEDIES THIS STATUTE ITSELF PROVIDES
For an employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, retaliated against, subjected to an adverse action, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment because of the statute's listed protected conduct, the statute itself entitles that employee to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts. Separately, an employer who willfully refuses to hire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee already determined eligible for rehiring or promotion through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or legally authorized hearing is guilty of a misdemeanor. In addition to other available remedies, an employer who violates this statute is also liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation, to be awarded to the employee or employees who suffered the violation.

  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(b)(1), reinstatement and reimbursement (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.6.)

  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(b)(3), civil penalty (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.6.)

THE 90-DAY REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION AND THE SEPARATE ONE-YEAR ADMINISTRATIVE COMPLAINT DEADLINE
If an employer takes an action this statute prohibits within 90 days of the employee's protected activity, California law creates a rebuttable presumption in the employee's favor — meaning the burden shifts to the employer to offer a non-retaliatory explanation for its action, not that retaliation is conclusively established. Separately, a different Labor Code section gives a person who believes they were discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of any law under the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction — which includes this statute — the option of filing an administrative complaint with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement within one year after the violation, a period the Labor Commissioner may extend for good cause. Filing that administrative complaint is not required before pursuing other rights and remedies under the law; the statute governing that administrative process states there is no exhaustion-of-administrative-remedies requirement.

  "Any person who believes that they have been discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of any law under the jurisdiction of the Labor Commissioner may file a complaint with the division within one year after the occurrence of the violation. The one-year period may be extended for good cause."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.7(a)(1), one-year administrative complaint deadline (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.7.)
  "In the enforcement of this section, there is no requirement that an individual exhaust administrative remedies or procedures."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 98.7(g), no exhaustion requirement (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=98.7.)

BEYOND THE EMPLOYEE DISCHARGED: APPLICANT AND FAMILY-MEMBER PROTECTIONS
The statute's protections are not limited to an employee who is already discharged. A job applicant who is refused employment, not selected for a training program leading to employment, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of an employment offer, because of the same categories of protected conduct addressed elsewhere in this document, is separately entitled to employment and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the prospective employer. The statute also separately prohibits an employer, or a person acting on the employer's behalf, from retaliating against an employee because that employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in protected conduct under this statute.

  "An employer, or a person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee because the employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter."

HOW THIS STATUTE DIFFERS FROM LABOR CODE § 132A'S WORKERS'-COMPENSATION-SPECIFIC SCHEME
Labor Code § 98.6, addressed throughout this document, is enforceable through a private civil action, and separately through an optional administrative complaint filed with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement under Labor Code § 98.7 — filing that administrative complaint is not a prerequisite to pursuing other remedies. citations.quote: An employer, or a person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee because the employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code § 98.6, addressed throughout this document, is enforceable through a private civil action, and separately through an optional administrative complaint filed with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement under Labor Code § 98.7 — filing that administrative complaint is not a prerequisite to pursuing other remedies. This is a structurally different enforcement path from this corpus's separate Workers' Compensation Retaliation (Labor Code § 132a) information sheet, which covers a statute that is instead enforced exclusively through a petition filed with, and adjudicated by, the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, subject to a one-year deadline running from the discriminatory act or date of termination, with the appeals board having no jurisdiction over any misdemeanor charge under that statute. The two statutes also protect different conduct: Labor Code § 98.6 protects wage-claim and Labor Commissioner-related activity, together with certain other Labor Code rights, while Labor Code § 132a protects the filing of, or testimony concerning, a workers' compensation claim.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 132a, closing paragraph — exclusive WCAB petition procedure and one-year deadline (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Proceedings for increased compensation as provided in paragraph (1), or for reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits, are to be instituted by filing an appropriate petition with the appeals board, but these proceedings may not be commenced more than one year from the discriminatory act or date of termination of the employee.
